The study focuses on estimating recurring labor costs for manufacturing an aircraft flap using RTM and VARTM liquid moulding processes.
RTM uses a closed mould with injection of resin under relatively high pressure into a dry preform.
VARTM uses vacuum to inject resin into a dry preform sealed with a vacuum bag on a single-sided tool.
The integral stiffened flap includes a flat skin, two tapered stiffeners, a tapered central blade stiffener, a central rib, and two gooseneck fittings.
Tapered stiffener design was chosen for its significant weight savings despite potentially higher tooling costs.
Process steps for RTM include tool preparation, preforming, injection and cure, finishing, and inspection.
Cost equations are based on MIT models using setup time (S), delay time (D), steady state velocity (S_v), dynamic time constant (D_t), part area, and number of parts.
Setup time (S) and delay time (D) were assumed zero for simplification in this preliminary study.
Cost constants D_t and S_v for tool preparation were estimated graphically using two data points: 15 minutes for the flap tool (7000 in²) and 3 minutes for a smaller fairing tool (100 in²).
VARTM requires additional vacuum bagging and distribution media steps not present in RTM.
VARTM recurring labor hours were found to be 10% greater than RTM, mainly due to vacuum bagging time.
Tool preparation times differ between RTM and VARTM due to tooling design differences.
The study uses a process flow chart approach to break down manufacturing into sub-processes and events for cost estimation.
The methodology aims to enable faster, more accurate conceptual design and manufacturing trade studies considering cost.
Future work includes extending the costing methodology to reinforced thermoplastic laminates and co-curing processes.
The research builds on Boeing's PCAD software approach for cost estimation of composite manufacturing.
The study assumes a single product per run, which affects the cost equation parameters.
The paper was published in 2002 in Composite Structures journal.
The research was conducted by Hawker de Havilland and Delft University.
The cost model accounts for geometry-related variables such as tool area and part area in estimating labor time.
